questions.enonce_markdown:
Determine the market price and give a reason for your answer.

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Method.** The **market (equilibrium) price** is the price at which the **quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied**. Compare the two columns of the schedule.

| Price (FCFA) | Qty demanded | Qty supplied | Situation |
|---|---|---|---|
| 600 | 100 | 700 | Surplus of 600 |
| 500 | 200 | 600 | Surplus of 400 |
| **400** | **300** | **300** | **Equilibrium** |
| 300 | 400 | 200 | Shortage of 200 |
| 200 | 500 | 100 | Shortage of 400 |
| 100 | 600 | 50 | Shortage of 550 |

**Answer.** The market price is **400 FCFA** per packet, and the equilibrium quantity is **300 packets**.

**Reason.** At 400 FCFA, **quantity demanded (300 packets) = quantity supplied (300 packets)**, so there is **neither a surplus nor a shortage**: buyers can buy all they want and sellers can sell all they offer. Above 400 FCFA supply exceeds demand and sellers cut the price, below 400 FCFA demand exceeds supply and the price is bid up, so the price returns to 400 FCFA.

![fig-1](gce-ol-economics-2021-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_3_fig_1.png)

questions.enonce_markdown:
The government guarantees sellers of biscuits a price of 600 FCFA:

(i) What name is given to this price? (2 marks)

(ii) State two consequences of the above price. (4 marks)

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Name of the price (2 marks)**

A price fixed by the government **above the equilibrium price** (400 FCFA) to protect sellers is a **minimum price**, also called a **price floor** or **guaranteed (support) price**. Sellers may not sell below it.

**(ii) Two consequences (4 marks)**

1. **A surplus (excess supply) appears.** At 600 FCFA sellers want to supply **700 packets** but buyers demand only **100 packets**, so there is a **surplus of $700 - 100 = 600$ packets**. Unsold stocks pile up. If the government buys the surplus at the guaranteed price, it spends $600 \times 600 = 360\,000$ FCFA, which is paid by taxpayers, and it must also bear **storage costs** (biscuits may expire and be wasted).

2. **Consumers pay a higher price and buy less.** The price rises from 400 to 600 FCFA and the quantity actually bought falls from 300 to 100 packets, so **consumers are worse off** and some people can no longer afford biscuits. Producers who sell receive a higher income, and the high price **encourages over-production** and a misuse of resources.

(Other acceptable consequences: possible black-market sales below the minimum price, and the need for the government to control stocks or exports.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
Calculate the price elasticity of supply, as price changes from 200 FCFA to 400 FCFA.

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Formula.**

$$PES = \frac{\%\ \text{change in quantity supplied}}{\%\ \text{change in price}}$$

**Data from the schedule.**

| Price (FCFA) | Quantity supplied |
|---|---|
| 200 | 100 |
| 400 | 300 |

**Calculation.**

- Change in quantity supplied: $300 - 100 = 200$, so $\%\Delta Q_s = \dfrac{200}{100} \times 100 = 200\%$
- Change in price: $400 - 200 = 200$, so $\%\Delta P = \dfrac{200}{200} \times 100 = 100\%$

$$PES = \frac{200\%}{100\%} = \mathbf{2}$$

**Interpretation.** $PES = 2$ is **greater than 1**, so supply is **elastic**: a 1% rise in price increases the quantity supplied of biscuits by 2%. (If the mid-point method is used, $PES \approx 1.5$, which is also elastic.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
Explain three factors that will influence the price elasticity of supply for biscuits.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The **price elasticity of supply (PES)** measures how responsive the quantity supplied of biscuits is to a change in their price. Three factors that influence it are as follows.

**1. Time period.** In the **short run** a bakery cannot quickly change its output (the ovens and the workers are fixed), so supply is **inelastic**. In the **long run** firms can buy more ovens, hire workers and new firms can enter, so supply becomes **more elastic**.

**2. Availability of spare capacity and of raw materials.** If the factory has **idle machines and workers** and can easily get **flour, sugar and packaging**, it can raise output quickly when the price rises, so supply is **elastic**. If it is already working at full capacity or flour is scarce, supply is **inelastic**.

**3. Ability to store the product (stocks).** Biscuits are **durable and can be stored**; producers hold stocks and release them on the market when the price rises, so supply is **fairly elastic**. For goods that quickly go bad (fresh fruit) supply is inelastic.

**Other factors:** the **mobility of factors of production** (how easily labour and capital can be moved to biscuit production), the **ease of entry** of new firms, and the **nature of the production process** (simple technology gives more elastic supply).

**Conclusion.** Supply of biscuits is more elastic when time is long, spare capacity and inputs are available and the product can be stored.
